'''Ground-level Building''' (Heichitatemono) is a style of {{ill|Building|en|Building|qid=Q41176|lt=Building|1=Building}} in which the construction uses the natural ground surface – or ground that has been only slightly embanked – as its {{ill|Floor|en|Floor|qid=Q217164|lt=Floor|1=Floor}}. In the archaeology of {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan|1=Japan}}, it is a concept used as a classification based on the level of the floor of the building’s {{ill|Feature (archaeology)|en|Feature (archaeology)|qid=Q814254|lt=Archaeological Feature|1=Feature (archaeology)}}. When a structure served as a {{ill|Apartment|en|Apartment|qid=Q188507|lt=Residence|1=Apartment}}, it is sometimes referred to as a '''Ground-level (type) Residence''' (Heichijūkyo) {{Sfn|石野|2006|pp=10-62}}.

==Overview==
It is used as a term to distinguish structures such as {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}} (pit dwellings), in which the floor is set below the natural ground surface by excavating into the earth, and {{ill|Raised-floor Building|de|aufgeständertes Gebäude|ja|高床建物|1=Raised floor building|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Building|qq=}}, which – among the {{ill|Post in ground|en|Post in ground|qid=Q1695743|lt=Pit-post Buildings|1=Post in ground}} – have their floors constructed above the ground surface {{Sfn|文化庁文化財部記念物課|2013|p=192}}. Since the designation is based on the criterion that the floor level is at or very near the ground surface, {{ill|Post in ground|en|Post in ground|qid=Q1695743|lt=Pit-post Building|1=Post in ground}}, as well as {{ill|Foundation|de|Fundament|ja|土台|lt=Foundation Building|lt_ja=土台建物|lt_de=Fundamentgebäude|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Foundation|1=Ground sill|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q11423103}} and {{ill|Cornerstone Building|de|Grundsteingebäude|ja|礎石建物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Cornerstone Building|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 礎石|1=Cornerstone|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q1133673}} (except for those with raised-floor structures), are in a broad sense also included under “ground-level buildings” {{Sfn|文化庁文化財部記念物課|2013|p=192}}.
It is also sometimes called a ground-level '''-style''' building, but<ref>{{Cite web|和書|author=国営吉野ヶ里歴史公園|url=https://www.yoshinogari.jp/ym/episode04/house.html|title=1.住まいと建築|work=弥生ミュージアム|accessdate=2022-10-31}}</ref> in contemporary Japanese archaeology, structures formerly designated as {{ill|Raised-floor Warehouse|de|aufgeständertes Lagerhaus|ja|高床式倉庫|1=Raised floor building|2=ja|3=高床式倉庫|lt=Raised-floor '''style''' Warehouse|lt_ja=高床'''式'''倉庫|lt_de=aufgeständertes Lagerhaus|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Warehouse|qq=}} or {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house '''style''' Dwelling|1=Pit-house}} have come to be called simply {{ill|Raised-floor Building|de|aufgeständertes Gebäude|ja|高床建物|1=Raised floor building|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Building|qq=}} (or raised-floor warehouse) and pit-house (or pit dwelling), respectively. Similarly, the practice of appending the suffix “style” has become uncommon {{Refnest|group=Note|In the 2010s, in the 'Guide to Excavation Survey' published by {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|en|Agency for Cultural Affairs|qid=Q1009519|lt=Agency for Cultural Affairs|1=Agency for Cultural Affairs}}, these building remains were uniformly recorded without the “style” suffix {{Sfn|文化庁文化財部記念物課|2013|pp=117-224}}.}}.

During the {{ill|Paleolithic|en|Paleolithic|qid=Q40203|lt=Paleolithic|1=Paleolithic}} of the Japanese archipelago, people pursued animals for food and led a nomadic life – living in temporary shelters such as {{ill|Tent|en|Tent|qid=Q170544|lt=Tent|1=Tent}} – so that the {{ill|Feature (archaeology)|en|Feature (archaeology)|qid=Q814254|lt=Archaeological Feature|1=Feature (archaeology)}} of structures such as {{ill|Apartment|en|Apartment|qid=Q188507|lt=Residence|1=Apartment}} were not preserved; consequently, confirmed cases of such structures are extremely rare{{Refnest|group=Note|Remains of definitively identified structures from that period have been found in only about 10 instances {{Sfn|堤|2009|pp=67-71}}.}}. However, at the [[:en:Tanamukaihara Site|Tanamukahara Site]] in {{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|en|Kanagawa Prefecture|qid=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture|1=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Sagamihara|en|Sagamihara|qid=Q209779|lt=Sagamihara City|1=Sagamihara}} {{ill|Chūō-ku, Sagamihara|en|Chūō-ku, Sagamihara|qid=Q1132074|lt=Chuo Ward|1=Chūō-ku, Sagamihara}}, a building (residential-type structure) featuring 12 {{ill|Posthole|de|Pfostenloch|ja|柱穴|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Posthole|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Posthole|qid=Q1742751}} – which is considered a ground-level building – was discovered, confirming that this type of structure existed as early as the Paleolithic {{Sfn|堤|2009|pp=67-71}}.
Although the typical dwelling form in settlements from the {{ill|Jōmon period|en|Jōmon period|qid=Q52824|lt=Jomon period|1=Jōmon period}} (when settled life began) through the {{ill|Heian period|en|Heian period|qid=Q193292|lt=Heian period|1=Heian period}} was recognized as {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}}, the discovery in 1985 (Shōwa 60) of remains of a ground-level wall-built structure at the Onda Site in {{ill|Yamagata Prefecture|en|Yamagata Prefecture|qid=Q125863|lt=Yamagata Prefecture|1=Yamagata Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashiokitama District, Yamagata|en|Higashiokitama District, Yamagata|qid=Q1155520|lt=Higashiokitama District|1=Higashiokitama District, Yamagata}} {{ill|Takahata, Yamagata|en|Takahata, Yamagata|qid=Q772103|lt=Takahata Town|1=Takahata, Yamagata}}, revealed that ground-level buildings coexisted with pit-houses even during the Jomon period {{Sfn|佐原|2005|p=292}}{{Sfn|石野|2006|pp=57-59}}.
Furthermore, at the {{ill|Kuroimine Site|en|Kuroimine Site|qid=Q11678001|lt=Kuroimine Site|1=Kuroimine Site}} in {{ill|Gunma Prefecture|en|Gunma Prefecture|qid=Q129499|lt=Gunma Prefecture|1=Gunma Prefecture}} and {{ill|Shibukawa, Gunma|en|Shibukawa, Gunma|qid=Q851492|lt=Shibukawa City|1=Shibukawa, Gunma}}, during the first half of the {{ill|6th century|en|6th century|qid=Q8090|lt=6th century|1=6th century}} (late {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|qid=Q459939|lt=Kofun period|1=Kofun period}}), an {{ill|Volcanic eruption|en|Volcanic eruption|qid=Q7692360|lt=eruption|1=Volcanic eruption}} of {{ill|Mount Haruna|en|Mount Haruna|qid=Q1191690|lt=Mount Haruna|1=Mount Haruna}} buried the settlement instantly under thick {{ill|Volcanic ash|en|Volcanic ash|qid=Q107099|lt=volcanic ash|1=Volcanic ash}}, preserving aspects of daily life (as reflected in the {{ill|archaeological remains|de|Archäologische Überreste|ja|遺構面|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/archaeological remains|1=archaeological contexts|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q114345798}}) without subsequent leveling. At that site, the number of ground-level buildings was overwhelmingly higher – 36 examples compared to 5 {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}} and 8 {{ill|Raised-floor Building|de|aufgeständertes Gebäude|ja|高床建物|1=Raised floor building|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Building|qq=}} – a point that should be considered when examining the building composition and settlement landscape of ancient communities {{Sfn|文化庁文化財部記念物課|2013|p=192}}.
Note that in Japanese archaeology the terms Ground-level Building, {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}}, and {{ill|Raised-floor Building|de|aufgeständertes Gebäude|ja|高床建物|1=Raised floor building|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Building|qq=}} are classification names based on the “height” of the floor, defined as follows:
# {{ill|Pit-house|en|Pit-house|qid=Q940435|lt=Pit-house|1=Pit-house}}: a structure whose floor is below the ground surface.
# Ground-level Building: a structure whose floor is at the natural ground level or raised only slightly by embankment.
# {{ill|Raised-floor Building|de|aufgeständertes Gebäude|ja|高床建物|1=Raised floor building|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Raised-floor Building|qq=}}: a structure in which a floor board is placed on {{ill|dug pillars|de|ausgehöhlte Pfeiler|ja|掘立柱|1=Postholes|2=ja|3=掘立柱|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/dug pillars|qq=}}, thereby elevating the floor above the ground surface.

Thus, a building supported by a main pillar driven into the ground – designated as {{ill|Post in ground|en|Post in ground|qid=Q1695743|lt=Pit-post Building|1=Post in ground}} – is classified as a Ground-level Building if its floor was at ground level at the time, and as a Raised-floor Building if it was elevated above the ground. For this reason, when listing detected remains in excavation reports such as the {{ill|Excavation Report|de|Ausgrabungsbericht|ja|発掘調査報告書|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Excavation Report|1=archaeological excavation report|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q85882528}}, the Agency for Cultural Affairs has pointed out that describing them with phrases like "'''Pit-post Building and Ground-level Building'''", "'''Pit-post Building and Raised-floor Building'''", or "'''{{ill|Wall-built Structure|de|Mauerbau|ja|壁建ち建物|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Wall-built Structure|1=Wall‑built Structure|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q120785472}} and Ground-level Building'''" – which juxtapose building names based on differing classification criteria as if they were entirely separate – is meaningless, and that the description should reflect these classification criteria {{Sfn|文化庁文化財部記念物課|2013|p=192}}.
